title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, & ggplot2
text: We looked at Anscombe’s quartet to see how datasets with similar summary statistics can look very different when graphed. We learned how to build plots with ggplot2, choose geoms for different questions, and show uncertainty in American Community Survey (ACS) estimates.

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, & ggplot2
text:
Key Concepts
A ggplot has three basic parts:

Data — the table being plotted
Aesthetics — variables mapped to things like x, y, and color with aes()
Geoms — the marks drawn on the graph, such as points, lines, or bars

Use + to add layers to a plot. For example, geom_point() makes a scatterplot, while geom_histogram() shows the distribution of one numeric variable.
A variable goes inside aes() if its values control the plot’s appearance: aes(color = reliability). A fixed color goes outside aes(): color = "steelblue".
ACS estimates have margins of error (MOEs). A large MOE means I should be careful when comparing estimates, especially for small areas.

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, & ggplot2
text:
Proving R Works
The chunk below uses a dataset included with R to make a scatterplot. If the graph appears on my published site, ggplot2 is working in Quarto.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    x = "Weight (1,000 pounds)",
    y = "Miles per gallon"
  )

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, & ggplot2

I am beginning to see how ggplot2 works: choose the data, map variables to the graph, and add a geom. When using Census data, I also need to pay attention to uncertainty instead of treating every estimate as an exact number.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text: First we had a quiz. Then reviewed the portfolio workflow and created a practice folder for in-class R work. We then learned the basic structure of R code, including objects, assignment, functions, arguments, comments, packages, and the console. We also introduced Census data through the American Community Survey (ACS) and used tidycensus to retrieve county-level data for Pennsylvania.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Key Concepts
R code can save a result in an object:
result <- filter(counties, population > 50000) result is the object that stores the output. <- is the assignment arrow. filter() is a function, also called a verb in dplyr. counties is the input data. population > 50000 is an argument. Anything after # is a comment and does not run.
The ACS is a survey of roughly 3% of U.S. households. It produces an estimate and a margin of error (MOE). The 1-year ACS is more current but only covers places with populations above 65,000, while the 5-year ACS covers smaller geographies such as tracts and block groups.
A GEOID is an identifier stored as text so it keeps leading zeros. For example, Pennsylvania GEOIDs begin with 42. Census data can be in:
Long/tidy format: one row for each geography-variable combination. Wide format: one row per geography, with each variable in a separate column.
Wide format is useful when I need to compare variables, such as population and income, side by side.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at the median gross rent across counties in North Carolina, and ask which communities are measured most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "NC"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B25064_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)

[1] 100   5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                             variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                            <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 37001 Alamance County, North Carolina  B25064_001     1007    28
2 37003 Alexander County, North Carolina B25064_001      745    36
3 37005 Alleghany County, North Carolina B25064_001      755   114
4 37007 Anson County, North Carolina     B25064_001      849    63
5 37009 Ashe County, North Carolina      B25064_001      774    39
6 37011 Avery County, North Carolina     B25064_001      791    68


The dataset contains 100 rows, which matches the 100 counties in North Carolina State.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                                estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                                  <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Chowan County, North Carolina            766   290    37.9
 2 Gates County, North Carolina             940   214    22.8
 3 Graham County, North Carolina            581   125    21.5
 4 Hyde County, North Carolina             1237   244    19.7
 5 Cherokee County, North Carolina          800   151    18.9
 6 Washington County, North Carolina        829   134    16.2
 7 Tyrrell County, North Carolina           612    95    15.5
 8 Alleghany County, North Carolina         755   114    15.1
 9 Transylvania County, North Carolina      909   109    12.0
10 Camden County, North Carolina           1220   142    11.6


The county with the largest relative margin of error is Chowan County, with a margin of error equal to 37.9% of its estimated median gross rent.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    51
2 Low confidence     13
3 Moderate           36


There are 51 high-confidence counties, 36 moderate-confidence counties, and 13 low-confidence counties.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                             myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                             <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 37001 Alamance County, North Carolina    1007     28 174286    NA
2 37003 Alexander County, North Carolina    745     36  36440    NA
3 37005 Alleghany County, North Carolina    755    114  11075    NA
4 37007 Anson County, North Carolina        849     63  21903    NA
5 37009 Ashe County, North Carolina         774     39  26831    NA
6 37011 Avery County, North Carolina        791     68  17643    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         51        173508.
2 Low confidence           8         11434.
3 Moderate                41         40097.


High-confidence counties have an average population of about 173,508 people, while low-confidence counties average about 11,434 people. Moderate-confidence counties average about 40,097 people. This shows a clear pattern: smaller counties tend to have less reliable ACS median gross-rent estimates.
Reflection: The ACS estimates of median gross rent are least reliable in several small North Carolina counties, especially Chowan, Gates, Graham, Hyde, Cherokee, Washington, and Tyrrell Counties. Chowan County has the largest relative margin of error: its estimated median gross rent is $766, with a margin of error of $290, or 37.9%. This means the published estimate has a large amount of uncertainty and should not be treated as a precise measure of what renters pay there. Gates and Graham Counties also have very high relative margins of error, at 22.8% and 21.5%, respectively.
This pattern occurs because the ACS is based on a sample rather than a complete count of every household. Smaller counties have fewer households in the survey sample, so their estimates are less stable and have larger margins of error. In contrast, counties with larger populations generally have more survey responses and therefore more reliable estimates. My results show that 51 North Carolina counties have high-confidence estimates, while 13 counties fall into the low-confidence category.
If a state agency allocated housing-assistance funding based only on these median-rent estimates, without considering their margins of error, it could make unfair decisions. Small counties with uncertain estimates could receive too little funding if their rent is underestimated, or funds could be directed inefficiently if rent is overestimated. Residents of rural counties, where housing data are already limited, would be most likely to be affected. Policymakers should therefore use ACS estimates together with their margins of error and avoid treating all county-level numbers as equally certain.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, & Coordinate Systems
text: We joined Census income data from different years using GEOID, then learned how spatial data stores geometry alongside a table. We discussed coordinate reference systems (CRS), map projections, and why distance calculations need appropriate units. We also introduced sf functions for finding tracts near stations and measuring spatial relationships.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, & Coordinate Systems
text: We joined Census income data from different years using GEOID, then learned how spatial data stores geometry alongside a table. We discussed coordinate reference systems (CRS), map projections, and why distance calculations need appropriate units. We also introduced sf functions for finding tracts near stations and measuring spatial relationships.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, & Coordinate Systems
text:
Key Concepts
A GEOID identifies a Census geography. It should be stored as text so leading zeros are preserved. When joining two tables, the GEOID columns need to refer to the same type of geography and use matching values.
A left_join() keeps every row from the first table and adds matching columns from the second. If a GEOID has no match, the new column contains NA. When the first table is an sf object, its geometry column stays attached.
sf stands for simple features. An sf table contains ordinary columns plus a geometry column with shapes such as points or polygons.
A CRS tells R how coordinates relate to places on Earth:



EPSG
CRS
Units




4326
WGS 84
Degrees


4269
NAD 83
Degrees


2272
Pennsylvania South State Plane
US survey feet


5070
NAD 83 / Conus Albers
Meters



A geographic CRS uses longitude and latitude. A projected CRS represents locations on a flat map, often in feet or meters. Projections involve tradeoffs: one may preserve local shapes, while another preserves areas or distances better for a particular purpose.
Use st_crs() to check a layer’s CRS. st_set_crs() assigns the correct existing CRS label when it is missing; it does not move coordinates. st_transform() converts coordinates into another CRS. I need to check the units before making a buffer or interpreting a distance.
Some useful spatial functions are:

st_buffer() creates an area around a feature.
st_filter() selects features with a spatial relationship, such as tracts that intersect station buffers.
st_intersection() creates the shared geometry where features overlap.
st_union() combines geometries into one shape.
st_join() adds attributes based on a spatial relationship.
st_distance() calculates distances between features.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, & Coordinate Systems
text:
Proving R Works
This example joins income data from two years by GEOID. The 2023 table goes first, so all three of its GEOIDs remain. GEOID "300" has no 2015 match and receives NA.

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

income_23 <- tibble(
  GEOID = c("100", "200", "300"),
  med_inc_23 = c(82000, 31500, 45000)
)

income_15 <- tibble(
  GEOID = c("100", "200", "400"),
  med_inc_15 = c(61000, 27000, 39000)
)

income_joined <- left_join(income_23, income_15, by = "GEOID")

income_joined

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  GEOID med_inc_23 med_inc_15
  <chr>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1 100        82000      61000
2 200        31500      27000
3 300        45000         NA


I can check the join by counting rows and missing values:

income_joined |>
  summarize(
    rows = n(),
    missing_2015_income = sum(is.na(med_inc_15))
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
   rows missing_2015_income
  <int>               <int>
1     3                   1


The result should show 3 rows and 1 missing 2015 income value. This example uses ordinary tables; a spatial version would also have a geometry column.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, & Coordinate Systems
text:
Reflection
I learned that joining Census data to a map depends on both the table key and the spatial data. A join can run successfully while still leaving unmatched GEOIDs, so I should check the row count and missing values afterward. I also understand why I need to check the CRS before making a half-mile buffer: the number supplied to st_buffer() only makes sense when I know the layer’s distance units.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, & Coordinate Systems
text:
Questions I Still Have

If Census tract boundaries change between 2015 and 2023, is matching by GEOID alone enough to compare income across years?
Should a tract count as near a station when any part of it touches a half-mile buffer, or only when its centroid falls inside?
When st_distance() returns distances to many stations, how do I find just the nearest station for each tract?

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text: New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 1: Reconstructing the Article’s Data
The article compares Philadelphia neighborhood poverty using the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS 5-year estimates. I use survey = "acs5" with year = 2010 and year = 2017 to retrieve those periods. The periods do not overlap, so they do not share collection years. For the change test, I use the standard approximation that the estimates from the two periods are independent.
I use table B17001: B17001_002 counts people below the poverty level, and B17001_001 counts people for whom poverty status is determined. Dividing these gives the poverty rate. I assume this measure corresponds to the article’s overall poverty measure. Because its neighborhood-to-tract definitions are unavailable, I compare Philadelphia census tracts rather than reconstructing its neighborhood totals. I match tracts by GEOID and assume matched tracts represent comparable areas; matching identifiers alone does not verify unchanged boundaries.


Show code
poverty_10 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = c(
    poor = "B17001_002",
    poverty_universe = "B17001_001"
  ),
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

poverty_17 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = c(
    poor = "B17001_002",
    poverty_universe = "B17001_001"
  ),
  year = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

dim(poverty_10)


[1] 384   6


Show code
dim(poverty_17)


[1] 384   6




Show code
poverty_10 <- poverty_10 %>%
  select(
    GEOID,
    poor_10E = poorE,
    poor_10M = poorM,
    universe_10E = poverty_universeE,
    universe_10M = poverty_universeM
  )

poverty_17 <- poverty_17 %>%
  select(
    GEOID,
    NAME,
    poor_17E = poorE,
    poor_17M = poorM,
    universe_17E = poverty_universeE,
    universe_17M = poverty_universeM
  )

poverty <- poverty_17 %>%
  left_join(poverty_10, by = "GEOID")

poverty %>%
  summarize(
    n_tracts = n(),
    no_2010_match = sum(is.na(poor_10E))
  )


# A tibble: 1 × 2

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 2: Testing Poverty Change


Show code
poverty <- poverty %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate_10 = poor_10E / universe_10E,
    poverty_moe_10 = moe_prop(
      poor_10E,
      universe_10E,
      poor_10M,
      universe_10M
    ),
    poverty_se_10 = poverty_moe_10 / 1.645,
    poverty_cv_10 = poverty_se_10 / poverty_rate_10 * 100,

    poverty_rate_17 = poor_17E / universe_17E,
    poverty_moe_17 = moe_prop(
      poor_17E,
      universe_17E,
      poor_17M,
      universe_17M
    ),
    poverty_se_17 = poverty_moe_17 / 1.645,
    poverty_cv_17 = poverty_se_17 / poverty_rate_17 * 100,

    reliability_17 = case_when(
      is.na(poverty_cv_17) ~ NA_character_,
      poverty_cv_17 < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      poverty_cv_17 <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE                ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )

poverty %>%
  summarize(
    n_tracts = n(),
    missing_2010_rate = sum(is.na(poverty_rate_10)),
    missing_2017_rate = sum(is.na(poverty_rate_17))
  )


# A tibble: 1 × 3

1      384                 7                 8

  geom_errorbar(

    width = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(color = change_result), size = 2.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Largest Estimated Changes in Philadelphia Tract Poverty",
    subtitle = "2006–2010 to 2013–2017: 10 largest increases and 10 largest decreases",
    x = "Census tract GEOID",
    y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)",
    color = "90% confidence test",
    caption = "Source: ACS 5-year estimates, B17001. Bars show 90% confidence intervals for change."
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









This figure shows the ten largest estimated increases and ten largest estimated decreases, rather than all 376 tracts. Error bars that cross zero indicate changes that are not statistically detectable at 90% confidence.
Tract 9891 illustrates the importance of uncertainty. Its estimated poverty rate increased by 23.3 percentage points, but the change’s margin of error is about 221 percentage points. Its poverty-status population estimates were only 68 and 53, with margins of error larger than those estimates. The resulting approximate interval extends beyond possible changes, indicating that this comparison is too imprecise to support a conclusion about the direction of change.


Show code
change_counts <- poverty_compare %>%
  count(change_result)

ggplot(
  change_counts,
  aes(x = change_result, y = n)
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Most Philadelphia Tracts Had No Detectable Poverty-Rate Change",
    subtitle = "2006–2010 compared with 2013–2017, using 90% confidence",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of census tracts",
    caption = "Source: ACS 5-year estimates, B17001. Includes 376 tracts with defined rates in both periods."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










What the results show
Of the 376 tracts included in the comparison, 36 showed a statistically detectable increase in poverty and 27 showed a detectable decrease at 90% confidence. The remaining 313 tracts, or 83.2%, showed no statistically detectable change. This does not mean their poverty rates stayed exactly the same. It means the estimated changes were not large enough relative to their uncertainty to distinguish them from zero.
The reliability table also shows that most tract poverty rates were only somewhat reliable. In 2006–2010, 11 tracts were classified as reliable, 321 as somewhat reliable, and 44 as unreliable. In 2013–2017, those counts were 22, 332, and 22. These categories describe the precision of each period’s poverty rate; they do not directly determine whether the change between periods is statistically detectable.
Overall, the results show increases in some tracts and decreases in others. They do not establish what happened in the specific neighborhoods named in the article, because the article’s neighborhood-to-tract definitions are unavailable. The tract counts also do not measure the change in Philadelphia’s overall poverty rate, since tracts contain different numbers of people.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
section: Part 3: Which Claims Does the Evidence Support?
text:
Part 3: Which Claims Does the Evidence Support?
Supported: The article reports that poverty increased in some parts of Philadelphia. My tract-level analysis supports that broad pattern: 36 tracts showed statistically detectable increases between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. However, 27 tracts showed detectable decreases, so the direction of change varied across the city. Not supported by this analysis: Treating every estimated increase as clear evidence that conditions worsened would overstate the findings. For example, Tract 9891 had an estimated increase of 23.3 percentage points, but its extremely large margin of error prevents a confident conclusion about the direction of change. Across all 376 comparable tracts, 313 changes were not statistically distinguishable from zero. This does not prove that poverty was unchanged in those places.
Cannot be determined: I cannot verify the article’s claim that Eastwick’s poverty rate rose from 12% to 26%, or that it had the largest neighborhood increase, because the article does not identify the tracts used to define each neighborhood. The same limitation prevents verification of Fairhill’s reported 61% poverty rate. My analysis also does not test the article’s claim about increasing poverty among white residents: the variables used here describe poverty across the full poverty-status population, not a specific racial group. Finally, these comparisons cannot establish the suggested causes of change, such as opioid use or migration. Those explanations would require additional evidence.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 4: A More Defensible Account
Philadelphia’s poverty trends varied across census tracts between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 American Community Survey periods. Among 376 tracts with usable poverty rates in both periods, 36 showed increases and 27 showed decreases that were statistically detectable at 90% confidence. For the other 313, uncertainty was too large to establish a change. These results indicate worsening poverty in some areas and improvement in others, rather than a uniform trend. They also show why a large estimated increase should not automatically be treated as a clear deterioration. The article’s exact figures for neighborhoods such as Eastwick and Fairhill cannot be verified through this tract-level analysis without knowing how the neighborhood boundaries were defined.

Part 3: Join by where
In Part 1b, the join failed because it matched on a label (GEOID), and the label changed. st_join() matches on location instead: a row is matched to whatever it sits on top of. Stations don’t have a GEOID column, and they don’t need one.
Every station gets its tract’s attributes:

stations_with_tract <- st_join(stations, philly_tracts)

stations_with_tract %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(name, GEOID, med_incE, reliability) %>%

The second route counts directly:

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%

section: Part 4: How far is the nearest station?
text:
Part 4: How far is the nearest station?
st_distance() returns a matrix, not a column. Look at its shape first:

centroids <- st_centroid(st_geometry(philly_tracts))

dim(st_distance(centroids, stations))

[1] 391 319


Instead, find the nearest station for each tract, then measure only that one distance:

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(centroids, stations)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    dist_ft = as.numeric(
      st_distance(centroids, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)
    ),
    dist_mi = dist_ft / 5280
  )

summary(philly_tracts$dist_mi)

 0.01893  0.15554  0.41382  1.84137  2.73916 10.93093

section: Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
text:
Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 2640) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = st_disjoint)

nrow(outside_zone)

[1] 162


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
Part 6: The Challenge
You now have three different definitions of “has access”:

Distance: the tract centroid is within X miles of a station (dist_mi)
Touch: the tract touches the half-mile zone at all (st_filter)
Coverage: at least Y% of the tract’s area is inside the zone (pct_covered)


Your team’s task

Define “low-income.” For example, you could use the bottom quartile of tract median income, or a dollar threshold. Pick one and write it down.
Define “access.” Choose one of the three definitions above and set its threshold.
Answer the question. Which low-income tracts lack access? Produce:

The count of low-income tracts without access
A map showing them (a geom_sf() layer plus the stations)
The reliability breakdown: of those tracts, how many have High / Moderate / Low reliability income estimates?

Defend one decision in 2–3 sentences. Why this access definition and not another? How would your count change if you used a different one?

+1





Before you present, discuss

If a tract is “low-income” with a CV of 45%, does it belong on your list? What would you tell Indego about it?
Your three access definitions give different counts. Which one would an Indego planner prefer? Which one would a neighborhood advocate prefer?

text:
If you’re curious

Indego stations have a totalDocks property. Does “access” mean the same thing next to a 10-dock station and a 35-dock station?
Replace the centroid with st_point_on_surface(). Does any tract’s distance change a lot? Why might a centroid fall in an odd place for some tract shapes?
Straight-line distance ignores the Schuylkill, I-95, and rail yards. Which tracts do you suspect are farther in practice than your map shows?
